title: The diagnostic value of cardiovascular magnetic resonance in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
authors: Huerxidan Sidike; Yashengjiang Maimaiti; Saimaitikari Abudubari; Biling Liang; Guochao Dai; Maimaitiaili Tuerxun; Taihui Yu; Wenjie Tang
abstract:
Limited studies compare the clinical applications and diagnostic values of cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) versus echocardiography in individuals with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM).
This study was performed to evaluate the diagnostic value of CMR in patients with HCM.
A retrospective study without prospective follow-up was performed on the data from 100 patients diagnosed with HCM from July 2018 to December 2021. All patients underwent echocardiography, CMR scans, and late gadolinium enhancement (LGE). Various parameters of CMR were measured and compared to those of echocardiography to evaluate the diagnostic value of CMR in the diagnosis of HCM.
CMR classified the patients into 6 major types based on the location of myocardial hypertrophy involvement: ventricular septal HCM (n = 43); apical HCM (n = 30); basal septal HCM (n = 4); mid-ventricular HCM (n = 13); mass‑like HCM (n = 1), and diffuse HCM (n = 9). There were 4 patients with symmetric HCM, 96 with asymmetric HCM, 41 with obstructive HCM, and 59 with non-obstructive HCM. The diagnostic accuracy rate of CMR and echocardiography for HCM was 100% and 61%, respectively, with a missed diagnosis rate of 39% (39/100). LGE showed delayed enhancement, which manifested as patchy or focal enhancement within the hypertrophied myocardium. The delayed enhancement area was limited to the hypertrophied myocardial region. CMR + LGE showed myocardial fibrosis at the apex in 62 patients. Echocardiography alone detected 17 patients apical HCM.
The combination of CMR with clinical symptoms may aid in the diagnosis and classification of HCM, as well as in the characterization of myocardial fibrosis. CMR appears to be superior to echocardiography in detecting missed CMR diagnoses. Further study is required to validate these findings.

title: Echocardiographic Assessment of Prognosis and Treatment Benefit After Mitral Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Repair.
authors: Ehsan Shahverdi; Mahkameh Rasouli; Ramtin Keshavarzi; Carsten Schneider; Mathias Lange
abstract:
Mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) can achieve substantial mitral regurgitation (MR) reduction in appropriately selected patients, yet outcomes after technically successful intervention remain heterogeneous. This variability has prompted interest in echocardiographic markers of limited treatment benefit. However, adverse prognosis after TEER and absence of benefit attributable to TEER are fundamentally different concepts, and most available imaging studies evaluate the former rather than the latter.
This state-of-the-art review summarizes evidence on echocardiographic assessment of prognosis and treatment response across the mitral TEER pathway, integrating baseline multichamber phenotyping, procedural and immediate hemodynamic assessment, longitudinal imaging, and evidence from randomized trials of TEER in secondary MR.
Baseline left ventricular remodeling and myocardial dysfunction, left atrial disease, pulmonary hypertension, right ventricular dysfunction and right ventricular-pulmonary arterial uncoupling, and tricuspid regurgitation identify greater cardiovascular disease burden and residual risk after TEER. Procedural assessment extends beyond residual MR to include transmitral pressure gradient, forward flow, and left atrial hemodynamics, whereas serial imaging characterizes subsequent ventricular, atrial, pulmonary, and right-heart trajectories. Persistent structural or hemodynamic abnormalities and absence of reverse remodeling should not be equated with irreversible disease or therapeutic futility. Randomized subgroup analyses in secondary MR have not consistently demonstrated significant treatment-effect modification by several adverse echocardiographic phenotypes; however, these analyses were not adequately powered to exclude clinically meaningful interactions. Moreover, COAPT excluded patients with extreme ventricular remodeling, markedly elevated pulmonary pressures, or advanced RV dysfunction, limiting generalizability to these populations. Differences among COAPT, MITRA-FR, and RESHAPE-HF2 further caution against defining a universal echocardiographic treatment-response phenotype.
Echocardiography is essential for defining MR mechanism and severity, characterizing multichamber cardiovascular disease, evaluating procedural results, and refining longitudinal risk assessment. However, current evidence does not establish a validated echocardiographic threshold or phenotype that reliably predicts absence of treatment benefit. Randomized subgroup findings require cautious interpretation because of limited statistical power and the exclusion of patients with the most advanced ventricular and pulmonary vascular disease. Future adequately powered comparative studies should evaluate heterogeneity of treatment effect across MR etiologies using standardized multichamber imaging and patient-centered outcomes.

title: High-Voltage Electrical Injury Presenting with ST-Segment Elevation and Transient Myocardial Dysfunction without Obstructive Coronary Artery Disease.
authors: Muhammed Erzurum; Vedat Erdinc; Tuğba Kapanşahin; Kerem Oz; Yeşim Akın
abstract: Electrical injury may cause various cardiac complications, including electrocardiographic (ECG) changes that mimic acute myocardial infarction. We present a 38-year-old man who developed cardiopulmonary arrest after exposure to a 25,000-volt electrical current. The admission ECG showed inferolateral ST-segment elevation, raising suspicion for acute myocardial infarction. Cardiac biomarkers were markedly elevated, and transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 35% with inferoposterolateral wall hypokinesia accompanied by moderate mitral regurgitation. Emergency coronary angiography demonstrated no significant obstructive coronary artery disease. The post-coronary angiography ECG showed greater than 50% resolution of the ST-segment elevation. A 24-hour follow-up ECG demonstrated near-complete resolution of the ST-segment abnormalities, while repeat echocardiography showed complete recovery of left ventricular systolic function, resolution of the previously detected regional wall motion abnormalities, and regression of mitral regurgitation to a trivial degree. Although ventricular function normalized within 24 hours, the patient subsequently developed dialysis-requiring acute kidney injury, neurological deterioration, suspected pneumonia, and refractory septic shock and died on hospital day 10. This case highlights that high-voltage electrical injury may present with ST-segment elevation despite the absence of obstructive coronary artery disease, accompanied by reversible myocardial dysfunction, emphasizing the importance of considering ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) mimics in the differential diagnosis.

title: Distinct patterns of vascular failure in COL1A1-associated osteogenesis imperfecta and FBN1-associated Marfan syndrome
authors: Hiroshi Kubota; Hidehito Endo; Masao Nunokawa; Toshihiko Isaji; Sachito Minegishi; Hiroshi Tsuchiya; Masaru Kimura; Toru Ikezoe; Yusuke Inaba; Yu Takahashi; Kouta Kogure; Tomohiro Iwakura; Yaeko Ichikawa; Yutaka Hosoi
abstract: Introduction Heritable connective tissue disorders are an important cause of aortic disease; however, the mechanisms of vascular failure in genetically defined aortopathies remain incompletely understood. Methods We analyzed the clinical course, imaging findings, and histopathologic features of two patients with clinically and genetically characterized connective tissue disorders: COL1A1-associated osteogenesis imperfecta and FBN1-associated Marfan syndrome. Results The COL1A1-associated patient developed multilevel arterial complications, including aortic regurgitation requiring aortic valve replacement at age 36, rupture of a dissected right common iliac artery in the same year, chronic type A aortic dissection requiring root, ascending, and arch replacement at age 54, and rupture of the infrarenal abdominal aorta at a diameter of only 30 mm. The FBN1-associated patient presented with type B aortic dissection at age 34 and subsequently developed progressive aneurysmal disease requiring staged thoracoabdominal replacement, total arch replacement for acute type A dissection, and aortic root replacement, followed by multiple peripheral vascular reconstructions. Histopathologic examination demonstrated valvular myxomatous degeneration in both cases. The aortic wall in both patients showed medial degeneration with fragmentation of elastic fibers. In addition, the COL1A1-associated patient demonstrated abdominal aortic wall thinning, with a minimum thickness of 1.25 mm. Conclusions These two patients exhibited contrasting longitudinal vascular courses despite some overlapping histopathologic findings. The COL1A1-associated OI patient experienced rupture of a dissected infrarenal aortic segment, whereas the FBN1-associated Marfan patient experienced repeated dissections followed by progressive vascular dilatation and multiple surgical reconstructions. These observations are descriptive and do not establish genotype-specific patterns or mechanisms of vascular failure.

title: Editorial: Management of arrhythmias in acute and intensive care settings
authors: Martin Balík; Štěpán Havránek
abstract: Cardiac arrhythmias become frequent in general population which transmits to the incidence among the critically ill. (1) As an independent mortality predictor, they represent either a primary problem or consequence of the underlying critical illness and an important driver of further hemodynamic deterioration. (2,3) The evidence in critical care arrhythmia management is limited because some of the conclusions generated on large cohorts of cardiology outpatients cannot be applied in the acute and intensive care setting. Hence, the decisions are often driven by available bedside imaging and applied physiology. (4) Shortened diastolic filling, loss of atrial contribution, irregular ventricular activation, increased myocardial oxygen demand, reduced coronary perfusion, and impaired ventricular function may all contribute to a rapid decline in cardiac output, particularly in patients with pre-existing ventricular dysfunction or limited cardiovascular reserve. (5,6) The resulting hypotension and congestion, sympathetic activation and myocardial ischemia in turn facilitate recurrent arrhythmia. Thus, a self-perpetuating cycle may develop in which arrhythmia aggravates hemodynamic compromise, while hemodynamic and metabolic deterioration further increases arrhythmogenicity. (5)(6)(7) Potentially reversible precipitants-including acute myocardial ischemia, electrolyte abnormalities, acidosis, hypoxemia, elevated filling pressure, infection, drug toxicity, and proarrhythmic medication-must be identified and corrected simultaneously.

title: Clinical outcome implications of novel auscultation device of artificial intelligence (NAVI-HF) in predischarge acute heart failure patients
authors: Rony Marethianto Santoso; Ser Wee; Amiliana Mardiani Soesanto; Wisnu Jatmiko; Aria Kekalih; Nuri Dyah Indrasari; Yong Kiang Yeo; Wilbert Huang; Bambang Budi Siswanto
abstract: Aim This study evaluated the prognostic significance of a novel auscultation device of artificial intelligence (NAVI-HF) in predicting clinical outcomes in predischarge acute heart failure (HF) patients. Methods This second, prognostic phase of a prospective observational cohort study extends our prior diagnostics phase, in which NAVI-HF demonstrated good performance compared with lung ultrasound (LUS) B-lines as the reference standard. Patients were classified as NAVI-HF positive or negative prior to discharge and followed for 6 months for evaluation. Results A total of 239 patients were included of whom 111 (45.1%) were NAVI-HF positive. NAVI-HF positive patients had a worse clinical profile and higher NT-proBNP ( p < 0.05). During a median follow-up of 6 months, 82 composite events (34.3%) occurred. In univariate Cox analysis, NAVI-HF positive was associated with significant increased risk of composite outcome (HR 1.59, CI 1.03–2.47; p 0.03) and HF hospitalization (HR 1.64, CI 1.05–2.46; p 0.02), but not all-cause mortality (p 0.24). The association in composite and HF hospitalization outcomes remained significant after adjustment for age and sex but was attenuated after adjustment for other prognostic variables. Conclusion NAVI-HF–detected congestion was associated with increased adverse clinical outcomes in predischarge acute HF patients.

title: Primary, atrial secondary, and ventricular secondary mitral regurgitation in the general population
authors: Laura Dorothea Keil; Alexander Hapfelmeier; Jan‐Per Wenzel; Julius Nikorowitsch; Daniel Kalbacher; Hermann C. Reichenspurner; Stefan Blankenberg; Evaldas Girdauskas
abstract: Abstract Background While primary mitral valve regurgitation (PMR) results from structural abnormalities of the mitral valve leaflets, secondary mitral valve regurgitation (SMR) arises from either mitral annular dilatation (atrial type, aSMR) or left ventricle remodelling (ventricular type, vSMR) in the absence of intrinsic leaflet disease. Although SMR is considered the most common cause of clinically relevant mitral regurgitation (MR), population-based data on its prevalence, subtype distribution, and clinical profiles are lacking. We aimed to determine the prevalence of PMR and SMR and to characterize PMR, aSMR, and vSMR in the general population. Methods We analyzed the first 10,000 participants of the population-based Hamburg City Health Study enrolled 2016–2019; 8543 echocardiographic examinations were available. Mitral valve morphology and function were independently assessed by two investigators. PMR was defined by the presence of intrinsic leaflet pathology, whereas SMR was classified as ventricular when left ventricular ejection fraction was less than 50% or less than 55% in the presence of geometric distortion (tenting area ≥ 150 mm 2 or coaptation depth ≥ 10 mm) and cases with left ventricular ejection fraction equal to or above 50% were classified as aSMR. Results A total of 216 participants had moderate or severe MR (2.53% of the total cohort, 95% confidence interval (CI): 2.20%–2.89%, see Fig. 3). Of these, 148 were classified as SMR (68.5%, 95% CI: 61.8%–74.7%), the remaining were mainly of primary etiology (31.5%, 95% CI: 25.3%–38.2%). Among SMR cases, aSMR was predominant (84.5%, 95% CI: 77.5%–89.9%), whereas vSMR accounted for 15.5% (95% CI: 10.1%–22.4%). Compared with aSMR, individuals with vSMR were older, more symptomatic, and more frequently had atrial fibrillation and hypertension. Echocardiographic parameters indicated more advanced cardiac remodelling and dysfunction in vSMR. Compared with SMR, participants with PMR had greater MR severity, while age and the proportion of women were numerically higher without reaching statistical significance. During a median follow-up of 4.56 years, 10 participants had died, with all-cause mortality being significantly higher among participants with PMR than among those with aSMR. Conclusion In this population-based cohort, SMR accounted for two-thirds of relevant MR, with aSMR being the predominant subtype. MR severity was higher in PMR as compared to SMR. Distinct echocardiographic and clinical profiles suggest more advanced disease in vSMR. Multivariate analysis revealed that atrial fibrillation was significantly more present in the vSMR cohort. These findings highlight the need for refined SMR subclassification and longitudinal studies to define prognostic implications and clinically meaningful definitions. All-cause mortality was highest in participants with PMR than in those with aSMR.

title: Case Report: When infection wears a rheumatic mask: probable systemic brucellosis mimicking seronegative inflammatory arthritis with sicca symptoms and suspected cervical spondylitis
authors: Yadan Zou; Jing Zhang; Xiaoying Zhang; Qiaolin Zhang; Lina Zhang; Ruohan Yu; Ting Long; Ji Li; Yanfeng Zhang; Shengguang Li
abstract: Background Brucellosis is a zoonotic infection with protean manifestations. Osteoarticular disease is common, but presentation as seronegative inflammatory arthritis with sicca symptoms, generalized lymphadenopathy, and cervical spondylitis may be mistaken for autoimmune rheumatic disease. Case presentation A 58-year-old male cattle farmer presented with intermittent chills, sicca symptoms, symmetric polyarthritis, weight loss, anemia, hypoalbuminemia, and elevated inflammatory markers. Autoimmune serology was negative. Ultrasonography confirmed synovial hyperplasia and tenosynovitis. 18F-FDG PET/CT showed generalized lymphadenopathy and focal C5 uptake; MRI showed C5 marrow edema. Lymph-node biopsy demonstrated non-necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with negative acid-fast and periodic acid-Schiff stains. Positive Rose Bengal and Brucella IgG tests, a standard tube agglutination titer of 1:100, and the clinical context prompted a working diagnosis of probable systemic brucellosis. Blood and bone marrow cultures were negative; paired serology was unavailable. At telephone follow-up, the patient reported taking outpatient rifampicin and doxycycline for 2 years, near-resolution of cervical pain at approximately 3 months, and normalization of inflammatory markers and hemoglobin after more than 6 months. A negative local agglutination result reported by his daughter at approximately 3 months could not be verified. Intermittent bilateral hip and knee pain persisted, requiring as-needed etoricoxib and, at the latest follow-up, a walking aid. Treatment had been extended because symptoms persisted, but the cause of the functional impairment remained undetermined. Conclusion Probable systemic brucellosis merits consideration in exposed patients with seronegative inflammatory arthritis, sicca symptoms, and granulomatous lymphadenopathy. Occupational seropositivity, incomplete microbiological confirmation, and unverified follow-up testing limit diagnostic certainty. Symptomatic improvement during antibiotics does not establish the etiology or microbiological cure, and persistent disability warrants reassessment for infection, structural disease, and coexisting rheumatic pathology.

title: A pathophysiology driven case based approach to managing pregnancy complicated by cardiac disease: Redefining the obstetrician’s role
authors: A. K. P. Ranaweera; S. Withanawasam; S. Marious; M. Nayanajith
journal: Sri Lanka Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology
abstract: Background: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a leading and potentially preventable cause of maternal morbidity and mortality. Management is complicated by the profound physiological adaptations of pregnancy, including increases in plasma volume, heart rate, stroke volume and cardiac output. Understanding the interaction between these physiological changes and the underlying cardiac condition enables obstetricians to anticipate clinical deterioration, individualize management and facilitate multidisciplinary care.Case presentation: This approach is illustrated by the case of a 27-year-old woman with Eisenmenger syndrome (modified World Health Organization class IV) who became pregnant despite medical advice and declined termination. Cardiovascular optimization, thromboprophylaxis, infection prevention, fetal surveillance, management of pre-eclampsia, management of fetal growth restriction, preterm caesarean delivery, intensive postpartum care and definitive contraception are the cornerstones of management. Conclusion: Management of CVD in pregnancy should be based on the pathophysiology of the underlying cardiac lesion and the cardiovascular demands imposed by pregnancy, labour and the puerperium. The obstetrician has a central role in integrating specialist recommendations into a coordinated plan that ensures maternal and fetal wellbeing.

title: Comparison of visual estimation of ventricular systolic function with quantitative echocardiographic markers in newborn infants
authors: Sujith S. Pereira; Beena Yeldo; Rachael Fleming; Saulius Šatas
abstract: BACKGROUND: Neonatologist-performed echocardiography (NPE) is increasingly practiced. NPE operators typically use visual estimation of systolic function and, if indicated, confirm function using quantitative echocardiographic markers. This exploratory study aims to compare the concordance between qualitative and quantitative echocardiographic markers among NPE and non-NPE operators. METHODS: We studied a cohort of newborn infants, undergoing routine NPE by the authors at Homerton University Hospital and Aberdeen Maternity Hospital from April 2024 to October 2024. Blinded NPE and non-NPE operators independently assessed left and right ventricular systolic function visually. We compared visual estimation with standard quantitative echocardiographic markers such as shortening fraction, Simpson's ejection fraction and global longitudinal strain for left ventricle and tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion and fractional area change for right ventricle. We examined the concordance between visual estimation and quantitative echocardiographic markers for biventricular systolic function. RESULTS: Sixty infants with a mean (SD) gestation and birth weight of 34 (6.2) weeks and 2311 (1319) grams respectively were examined. Sensitivity testing for all echocardiographic parameters ranged from 25% to 80% whereas specificity ranged from 38% to 78%. Sensitivity increased with worsening grades of LV dysfunction defined using shortening fraction. While concordance between NPE and non-NPE operator was generally limited across most echocardiographic parameters, test-retest reliability was acceptable for several quantitative measures, including Simpson's ejection fraction, global longitudinal strain and right ventricular fractional area change. CONCLUSION: Visual estimation may be a useful bedside tool for detecting severe ventricular dysfunction in newborn infants; however; quantitative echocardiographic measures are likely to improve the assessment of mild to moderate dysfunction. Further studies should confirm these findings in a larger cohort with a higher representation of infants with ventricular dysfunction.

title: Visual laryngeal mask for intraoperative ventilation in mitral valve surgery with tuberculous destroyed lung: a case report
authors: Aiting Lin; Huan Li; Xiaodong Cai; Jingli Lin; Kangcong Zhang; J Chen; Xuexian Tang; Lixin Chen; RuiYu Li; Jianjun Zhang; Ganghua Yang
abstract: Tuberculous destroyed lung (TDL) represents a severe, irreversible sequela of chronic pulmonary tuberculosis, characterized by extensive parenchymal destruction, fibrosis, and volume loss that results in significant ventilatory dysfunction. When complicated by rheumatic mitral valve disease (RMVD), these patients present formidable challenges for intraoperative respiratory management and surgical safety, particularly under cardiopulmonary bypass. We report a 56-year-old female with left TDL complicated by severe mitral regurgitation and moderate mitral stenosis. She underwent biological mitral valve replacement, tricuspid annuloplasty, left atrial appendage amputation, and pulmonary vein isolation under cardiopulmonary bypass. A visual laryngeal mask airway was innovatively adopted for intraoperative respiratory maintenance as an alternative to traditional endotracheal intubation. The device was removed immediately upon conclusion of the procedure. Despite the patient's unilateral effective pulmonary ventilation, stable oxygenation and ventilation were maintained throughout the operation. Postoperatively, the patient developed a mild right pleural effusion, which was relieved by thoracentesis; no severe respiratory complications such as hypoxemia or acute respiratory distress syndrome occurred. She was discharged on postoperative day 26. A 3-month follow-up demonstrated good recovery of both cardiac and respiratory function. This case highlights the clinical value of the visual laryngeal mask airway for intraoperative respiratory management in patients with TDL complicated by cardiac valve disease. It further emphasizes the importance of multidisciplinary team (MDT) collaboration and fast-track anesthesia principles in preoperative evaluation, surgical planning, intraoperative management, and postoperative complication control for such high-risk patients.

title: Transcatheter versus surgical closure of CHDs in predominantly pediatric populations: a systematic review of comparative and single-arm evidence
authors: Ali Majed; Pia Kmeid; Ayah Safa; Hamza Kahwaji; Abed El Rahman Naamani; Mohamad El-Atat; Amin Ossaily; Georges Ghanem
abstract: BACKGROUND: Transcatheter closure increasingly replaces surgery for congenital heart defects (CHDs), but comparative evidence comes almost entirely from atrial septal defect. We asked whether its trade-offs hold for other lesions in predominantly pediatric cohorts. METHODS: We searched PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL to June 2026 for cohorts with mean or median age under 18 years (PRISMA 2020). Only direct comparisons informed comparative conclusions. Narrative synthesis was stratified by lesion, with sensitivity analyses for mixed-age cohorts and adverse-event definitions. RESULTS: Six of eleven studies compared both approaches (1,158 transcatheter, 490 surgical patients), in atrial septal defect, patent ductus arteriosus, and coronary artery fistula; none addressed muscular ventricular septal defect. Procedural success was high with both. Hospital stay was shorter after transcatheter closure in all six (2.4-4.4 days in atrial septal defect), the most consistently observed finding. Major adverse events were less frequent after transcatheter closure in atrial septal defect, but arms differed in age and weight, and the difference was inconsistent in wholly pediatric cohorts; in coronary artery fistula, one study at serious risk of bias found them over twice as frequent after transcatheter closure. Where both arms were followed, reintervention was uncommon in each. GRADE certainty was low for hospital stay and procedural success, otherwise very low. CONCLUSIONS: Shorter hospital stay after transcatheter closure is the most consistently observed finding, at low certainty. Neither approach is shown to be safer: safety findings differed between lesions and, beyond atrial septal defect, rest on single studies. Lesion anatomy determines which approach applies.

title: Acute Angina in Anomalous Left Main Coronary Artery With Prepulmonic Course: A Case Report
authors: Mohammad Rouzbahani; Sepehr Navabifar; Nafiseh Montazeri; Amirmasoud rahimi; Alireza Hayati
abstract: Although a prepulmonic left main coronary artery is usually considered a lower-risk AAOCA subtype, it may still be associated with acute ischemic symptoms when significant atherosclerotic coronary artery disease is present. Multimodality imaging is essential for defining the coronary anatomy, and coronary artery bypass grafting may be the preferred strategy when severe multivessel disease coexists.

title: Decompensated Rheumatic Mitral Stenosis in the Context of Pregnancy and Atrial Fibrillation: A Case Report
authors: Rohith Narayan Narayanaswamy Yechanahally; Timothy Swinn; Laisha Gogola; Amardeep Ghosh Dastidar
abstract: We report a case of a 36-year-old Indian origin woman who presented with heart failure (HF) and atrial fibrillation (AF).She was found to be pregnant on admission, which she was unaware of, and further biochemical testing confirmed that she had a miscarriage.Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) revealed severe rheumatic mitral stenosis (MS), and transoesophageal echocardiography (TOE) demonstrated a left atrial appendage (LAA) thrombus.This case highlights the importance of echocardiography in diagnosing rheumatic heart disease (RHD) and in identifying complications.Furthermore, it demonstrates the challenges of managing decompensated MS in the context of pregnancy and AF.

title: Multivalvular Infective Endocarditis Presenting as Complete Heart Block and Neurological Features Mimicking Meningoencephalitis
authors: Amaan Khan; Maryam Saad Ahmadzai; Fatima Saad; Sophie Wilkinson; Andy Thornley
abstract: A 34-year-old man was admitted with fever, cough, chest pain, headache, and acute confusion, raising an initial suspicion of meningoencephalitis.However, two sets of blood cultures obtained before empirical antibiotic therapy grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA), and an electrocardiogram showed complete heart block.His condition deteriorated rapidly, progressing to respiratory failure and cardiogenic shock.Cardiac imaging demonstrated multivalvular infective endocarditis with severe mitral regurgitation secondary to perforation of the mitral leaflet.Emergency valve surgery was undertaken, followed by permanent pacing.This case emphasises the importance of early cardiac assessment in patients with systemic infection and conduction abnormalities, as it highlights an atypical presentation of infective endocarditis mimicking neurological infection.

title: Heart transplantation for rapidly progressive dilated cardiomyopathy complicated by an inferolateral left ventricular aneurysm: a case report
authors: Zhihua Yu; Li Yang; Ye Xu; Zuomin Li; Lijun Wang; Liqun He
abstract: Background Left ventricular (LV) aneurysm most commonly follows transmural myocardial infarction and is rarely described in dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM). When DCM and ischemic injury coexist, the presentation may be atypical and progression can be rapid. Case summary A 52-year-old man developed chest tightness and dyspnea after an upper respiratory tract infection. Echocardiography showed LV dilatation with reduced systolic function (LVEF 36%). Coronary angiography on hospital day 4 demonstrated severe stenoses of the left circumflex/obtuse marginal branch and a moderate right coronary artery lesion, and a drug-eluting stent was implanted in the left circumflex artery. One month later, he was readmitted with recurrent dyspnea, BNP 2,627 ng/L, complete left bundle branch block, marked LV dilatation (end-diastolic diameter 113 mm), severe functional mitral regurgitation, and a large inferolateral apical LV aneurysm (74 mm × 50 mm) with paradoxical motion. Despite intensified heart failure therapy, he progressed to end-stage heart failure and underwent heart transplantation. Histopathology of tissue adjacent to the aneurysm was consistent with myocardial infarction with chronic inflammatory cell infiltration, and the sampled left circumflex artery showed atherosclerotic stenosis. Conclusion In DCM with new regional wall motion abnormalities or rapid structural deterioration, concomitant ischemic injury should be considered even when symptoms are non-specific. Electrical and mechanical dyssynchrony may increase regional wall stress and contribute to aneurysm formation, accelerating clinical decline.

title: Predicting hypertension risk using machine learning, deep learning, and quantum neural network models: a comparative evaluation
authors: Muhammad Usman Aslam; Songhua Xu; Sajid Hussain; Umair Arif; Musaddiq Ibrahim; Mohammad Hanan Saeed; Nafiu Lukman Abiodun
abstract: Hypertension is a major public health problem and an important risk factor for cardiovascular disease. Early identification of patients at risk of hypertension can support timely prevention and clinical assessment. This study developed and compared statistical, machine learning, deep learning, and quantum neural network (QNN) models for hypertension prediction using clinical data from 624 patients at District Headquarters Hospital, Faisalabad, Pakistan. The proposed framework involved data preprocessing, K-nearest neighbor imputation, chi-square-based feature selection, feature scaling, and synthetic minority over-sampling technique (SMOTE) for class balancing. Logistic regression was used as a statistical reference, while SVM, random forest, XGBoost, Naive Bayes, ANN, SVM with PCA, DNN, and QNN were evaluated. Stratified 10-fold cross-validation was used to assess model performance using accuracy, F-measure, AUC, precision, recall, specificity, and maximum probability of correct decision (MPCD). The DNN model achieved the highest accuracy (95.77%), while the QNN achieved the highest AUC (95.40%), precision (96.26%), and recall (94.76%). Naive Bayes showed the lowest accuracy (83.40%). The QNN was included as an exploratory hybrid quantum-classical approach using a simulated quantum circuit, and the results do not imply a quantum advantage over classical models. Overall, the evaluated models showed promising predictive performance for hypertension classification in the study population. Further evaluation using independent populations, external validation, and prospective clinical studies is needed before considering their use in routine clinical practice.

title: Case Report: Diabetic ketosis-associated hemichorea-hemiballism in an elderly patient with longstanding poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus
authors: Wennan Zhang; Lili Xu; Fu Xinzhi; Fengyao Sun; Yangang Wang
abstract: Hemichorea-hemiballism associated with ketotic hyperglycemia is a rare movement disorder. We report a case of right-sided hemichorea-hemiballism occurring in the setting of diabetic ketosis in a 70-year-old man with a 15-year history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus. The patient presented with subacute involuntary choreiform movements of the right limbs, accompanied by foot pain, significant weight loss, and multiple diabetic complications. Intensive insulin therapy combined with short-term symptomatic treatment resulted in rapid resolution of ketonuria, stabilization of blood glucose, and marked improvement of the movement disorder. Notably, brain MRI showed no classic striatal T1 hyperintensity. At the 3-month follow-up, the patient remained free of choreiform movements. This case highlights that diabetic ketosis can trigger hemichorea-hemiballism in elderly patients even in the absence of typical imaging findings, and underscores the central role of prompt glycemic optimization

title: EXPRESS: Ebstein’s anomaly in two cats, including a rare variant with partial anterior tricuspid leaflet displacement
authors: Gangshi Li; Xiaoyan Wang; Ting Yuan; Zihao Gan; Siqi Li; Yaoshun Peng; Aftab Shaukat
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery Open Reports
abstract: Case Summary Case 1: A 5‑month‑old male Ragdoll cat demonstrated acute anorexia, mild tachypnoea, and dull mentation. Cardiac auscultation revealed a grade 4/6 systolic murmur at the right cardiac apex. Echocardiography revealed marked right atrial enlargement, apical displacement of the tricuspid valve leaflets, and partial atrialization of the right ventricle, which were consistent with Ebstein’s anomaly (EA). Medical treatment was discontinued at the owner's request after 1 month. The cat remained relatively stable for several months but died from heart failure 16 months after the initial diagnosis. Necropsy confirmed apical displacement of the tricuspid septal leaflet and partial displacement of the anterior leaflet. Case 2: A 4-year-6-month-old spayed female domestic cat presented with lethargy, hyporexia, and acute tachypnea. Echocardiography revealed marked right atrial enlargement, apical displacement of the tricuspid septal leaflet, severe tricuspid regurgitation (peak regurgitant velocity 2.8 m/s), and partial atrialization of the right ventricle, which confirmed the diagnosis of EA. Clinical signs improved following medical treatment; however, the cat died at home 1 month later. Necropsy was declined, and the cause of death remained undetermined. Relevance and Novel Information This report describes two cases of feline EA and documents a rare morphological variant involving partial displacement of the anterior tricuspid leaflet. These findings expand current knowledge of anatomical variation in feline EA and may have implications for diagnosis and interpretation of echocardiographic findings.

title: EXPRESS: A Complex Aortic Coarctation with Ventricular Septal Defect and Patent Ductus Arteriosus in a Kitten
authors: Takashi Baba; Takanori Ando; Aoi Kosai; Shu Nakao
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery Open Reports
abstract: Case summary: A 6-day-old female domestic shorthair kitten weighing 140 g was presented with poor nursing and severe cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. Initial echocardiography revealed bilateral atrial enlargement, a membranous ventricular septal defect (VSD), and aortic narrowing. Follow-up assessment demonstrated progression of cardiomegaly and identification of a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). On day 48, multidetector CT confirmed a focal, severe narrowing of the aorta between the origin of the left subclavian artery and the insertion of the ductus arteriosus, consistent with aortic coarctation with concurrent VSD and PDA. Owing to the extremely low birth weight, surgical intervention was not feasible, and medical management was continued. The kitten developed transient atrial fibrillation on day 72, which resolved with diltiazem. Despite comprehensive medical therapy, refractory congestive heart failure recurred, and the kitten died on day 160. Postmortem examination confirmed focal aortic narrowing adjacent to a cylindrical PDA, marked biatrial dilatation, biventricular concentric hypertrophy, a membranous VSD and a right atrial mural thrombus. Histopathology of the pulmonary artery and PDA demonstrated elastic artery-like remodelling, consistent with chronic haemodynamic loading and secondary pulmonary hypertension. Relevance and novel information: aortic coarctation is an exceptionally rare congenital cardiovascular anomaly in cats. This report describes the clinical presentation and detailed postmortem characterisation of aortic coarctation with concurrent VSD and PDA in a kitten, highlights the diagnostic utility of advanced antemortem imaging, and illustrates the limitations of medical management in the presence of complex structural disease.

title: Obstructive Giant Left Atrial Myxoma Concurrent with Very High-Risk Acute Coronary Syndrome Presenting as Cardiogenic Shock: A Rare Dual Pathology
authors: Muhammad Rizky Felani; Maria Lerista; Sandy Hasan; Aswin Nugraha; Andina Dewanty
abstract: Background: Primary cardiac tumors are exceptionally rare, with cardiac myxomas being the most common benign type, typically originating in the left atrium. Despite their benign histopathological nature, these tumors can lead to serious complications, including intracardiac obstruction, embolic events, and even sudden cardiac death. The coexistence of a Left Atrial (LA) myxoma and Coronary Artery Disease (CAD) is an unusual clinical finding. This report highlights the importance of recognizing cardiac myxoma as a potential contributor to high-risk acute coronary syndrome and hemodynamic instability. Case Illustration: A 57-year-old man presented with recurrent chest pain and shortness of breath, consistent with very high-risk Non–ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI) and cardiogenic shock. Transthoracic Echocardiography (TTE) revealed a large LA mass causing functional mitral valve obstruction, highly suggestive of a myxoma. Further evaluation with transesophageal echocardiography confirmed a giant, highly mobile mass intermittently occluding the mitral inflow. Coronary angiography revealed significant Two-Vessel Coronary Artery Disease (CAD2VD), including chronic total occlusion of the Left Circumflex Artery (LCx). The patient subsequently underwent urgent combined surgical excision of the tumor and Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG). Histopathological examination confirmed the diagnosis of cardiac myxoma. The postoperative course was uneventful, with marked clinical improvement, complete resolution of symptoms, and preserved ventricular function on follow-up echocardiography. Conclusions: This case of very high-risk NSTEMI with cardiogenic shock was further complicated by a large LA myxoma causing dynamic mitral obstruction and diastolic inflow collapse. Early recognition using multimodal imaging and prompt surgical management are essential to prevent catastrophic hemodynamic deterioration and improve patient outcomes.
